bbe_format: True/False statements (usually A–E; questions 51–55 use A–F). Difficulty rated 1/5 to 5/5.

tasks.title: Multiple-Choice Guessing
tasks.context: A 10-question multiple-choice exam has 4 answer choices per question (1 correct). Person A guesses every answer at random (p = 0.25). Person B has studied and knows the material well (p = 0.90). To pass, a person needs at least 7 correct out of 10. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Person A's probability of scoring a perfect 10/10 by guessing is less than 0.01%.
The probability that Person B passes (scores at least 7 out of 10) equals the sum, from x = 7 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.90.
Person B is at least 300 times as likely as Person A to pass the exam.
Person B has a higher variance in number of correct answers than Person A.
Person A's mean (expected) number of correct answers is exactly one-fourth of the total number of questions.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Person A's probability of scoring a perfect 10/10 by guessing is less than 0.01%. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.25$ and $n = 10$:

$$P(X = 10) = (0.25)^{10} \approx 9.5367 \times 10^{-7} \approx 9.5367 \times 10^{-5}\%$$

The claim compares this with $0.01\%$. We got about $9.5367 \times 10^{-5}\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is True.

**B.** The probability that Person B passes (scores at least 7 out of 10) equals the sum, from x = 7 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.90. → True

“At least 7 out of 10” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 7, 8, \ldots, 10$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 7) = P(X=7) + P(X=8) + \cdots + P(X=10) = \sum_{x=7}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 7)$ would only capture “exactly 7” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.9$, running from $x = 7$ to $x = 10$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Person B is at least 300 times as likely as Person A to pass the exam. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 7 successes out of 10. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 7, 8, \ldots, 10$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 7) = \sum_{x=7}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 7)$ would only count “exactly 7” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.25$):

$$\binom{10}{7}(0.25)^{7}(0.75)^{3} \approx 0.0031$$

$$\binom{10}{8}(0.25)^{8}(0.75)^{2} \approx 0.0004$$

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.25)^{9}(0.75)^{1} \approx 2.861 \times 10^{-5}$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.25)^{10}(0.75)^{0} \approx 9.5367 \times 10^{-7}$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 7) \approx 0.0031 + 0.0004 + 2.861 \times 10^{-5} + 9.5367 \times 10^{-7} = 0.0035 \approx 0.35\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.9$):

$$\binom{10}{7}(0.9)^{7}(0.1)^{3} \approx 0.0574$$

$$\binom{10}{8}(0.9)^{8}(0.1)^{2} \approx 0.1937$$

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.9)^{9}(0.1)^{1} \approx 0.3874$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.9)^{10}(0.1)^{0} \approx 0.3487$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 7) \approx 0.0574 + 0.1937 + 0.3874 + 0.3487 = 0.9872 \approx 98.72\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 7)}{P_A(X \ge 7)} \approx \frac{98.72\%}{0.35\%} \approx 281.6$$

Since $281.6 \le 300$, the statement is False.

**D.** Person B has a higher variance in number of correct answers than Person A. → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.25$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 10 \cdot 0.25 \cdot 0.75 = 1.875$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.9$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 10 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.1 = 0.9$$

So $\mathrm{Var}(A) = 1.875$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 0.9$. The claim’s comparison is incorrect, so the statement is False.

**E.** Person A's mean (expected) number of correct answers is exactly one-fourth of the total number of questions. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 10 \cdot 0.25 = 2.5$$

$$E[B] = 10 \cdot 0.9 = 9$$

The difference $E[B] - E[A] = 6.5$, and equivalently $n(p_B - p_A) = 10\cdot(0.9 - 0.25) = 6.5$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.
tasks.solution_overview:
A 10-question multiple-choice exam has 4 answer choices per question (1 correct). Person A guesses every answer at random (p = 0.25). Person B has studied and knows the material well (p = 0.90). To pass, a person needs at least 7 correct out of 10.

We model each side as a binomial count with $n = 10$ independent trials: side A has success probability $p_A = 0.25$, side B has $p_B = 0.9$.

The scenario’s success cutoff is at least $k = 7$ successes out of $n = 10$.

tasks.title: Free Throws — Rookie vs All-Star
tasks.context: A basketball player takes 10 free throws. Player A is a rookie (p = 0.55 per shot). Player B is an all-star (p = 0.85 per shot). A "clutch" bonus is awarded for making at least 8 of the 10 shots. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Player B (the all-star) has more than a 20% chance of making all 10 shots in a row.
The probability that Player A earns the clutch bonus (at least 8 of 10 made) equals the sum, from x = 8 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.55.
Player B is more than 9 times as likely as Player A to earn the clutch bonus.
Player A's results have a larger standard deviation than Player B's.
The expected number of made shots for Player B is exactly 3 more than for Player A.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Player B (the all-star) has more than a 20% chance of making all 10 shots in a row. → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.85$ and $n = 10$:

$$P(X = 10) = (0.85)^{10} \approx 0.196874 \approx 19.69\%$$

The claim compares this with $20\%$. We got about $19.6874\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** The probability that Player A earns the clutch bonus (at least 8 of 10 made) equals the sum, from x = 8 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.55. → True

“At least 8 out of 10” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 8, 9, \ldots, 10$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 8) = P(X=8) + P(X=9) + \cdots + P(X=10) = \sum_{x=8}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 8)$ would only capture “exactly 8” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.55$, running from $x = 8$ to $x = 10$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Player B is more than 9 times as likely as Player A to earn the clutch bonus. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 8 successes out of 10. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 8, 9, \ldots, 10$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 8) = \sum_{x=8}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 8)$ would only count “exactly 8” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.55$):

$$\binom{10}{8}(0.55)^{8}(0.45)^{2} \approx 0.0763$$

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.55)^{9}(0.45)^{1} \approx 0.0207$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.55)^{10}(0.45)^{0} \approx 0.0025$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 8) \approx 0.0763 + 0.0207 + 0.0025 = 0.0996 \approx 9.96\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.85$):

$$\binom{10}{8}(0.85)^{8}(0.15)^{2} \approx 0.2759$$

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.85)^{9}(0.15)^{1} \approx 0.3474$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.85)^{10}(0.15)^{0} \approx 0.1969$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 8) \approx 0.2759 + 0.3474 + 0.1969 = 0.8202 \approx 82.02\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 8)}{P_A(X \ge 8)} \approx \frac{82.02\%}{9.96\%} \approx 8.24$$

Since $8.24 \le 9$, the statement is False.

**D.** Player A's results have a larger standard deviation than Player B's. → True

The standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance. For $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$,

$$\mathrm{SD}(X) = \sqrt{np(1-p)}$$

Side A ($p_A = 0.55$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 2.475, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(A) = \sqrt{2.475} \approx 1.573$$

Side B ($p_B = 0.85$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 1.275, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(B) = \sqrt{1.275} \approx 1.129$$

Comparing $1.573$ with $1.129$, the statement is True.

**E.** The expected number of made shots for Player B is exactly 3 more than for Player A. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 10 \cdot 0.55 = 5.5$$

$$E[B] = 10 \cdot 0.85 = 8.5$$

The difference $E[B] - E[A] = 3$, and equivalently $n(p_B - p_A) = 10\cdot(0.85 - 0.55) = 3$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

tasks.title: Factory Batch Certification
tasks.context: A factory runs a quality check on 20 items per batch. Inspector A is newly trained (p = 0.75 of correctly classifying each item). Inspector B is experienced (p = 0.95). Certification for a batch requires correctly classifying at least 18 of the 20 items. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Inspector A's probability of a flawless run (correctly classifying all 20 items) is less than 0.2%.
The probability that Inspector A certifies the batch (at least 18 of 20 correct) equals the sum, from x = 18 to 20, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 20 and p = 0.75.
Inspector B is at least 10 times as likely as Inspector A to certify the batch.
Inspector A's variance in number of correctly classified items is more than 4 times Inspector B's variance.
On average, Inspector A does not meet the certification bar of 18 correctly classified items.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Inspector A's probability of a flawless run (correctly classifying all 20 items) is less than 0.2%. → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.75$ and $n = 20$:

$$P(X = 20) = (0.75)^{20} \approx 0.003171 \approx 0.32\%$$

The claim compares this with $0.2\%$. We got about $0.3171\%$, which is above the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** The probability that Inspector A certifies the batch (at least 18 of 20 correct) equals the sum, from x = 18 to 20, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 20 and p = 0.75. → True

“At least 18 out of 20” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 18, 19, \ldots, 20$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 18) = P(X=18) + P(X=19) + \cdots + P(X=20) = \sum_{x=18}^{20} \binom{20}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{20-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 18)$ would only capture “exactly 18” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 20$ and $p = 0.75$, running from $x = 18$ to $x = 20$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Inspector B is at least 10 times as likely as Inspector A to certify the batch. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 18 successes out of 20. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 18, 19, \ldots, 20$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 18) = \sum_{x=18}^{20} \binom{20}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{20-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 18)$ would only count “exactly 18” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.75$):

$$\binom{20}{18}(0.75)^{18}(0.25)^{2} \approx 0.0669$$

$$\binom{20}{19}(0.75)^{19}(0.25)^{1} \approx 0.0211$$

$$\binom{20}{20}(0.75)^{20}(0.25)^{0} \approx 0.0032$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 18) \approx 0.0669 + 0.0211 + 0.0032 = 0.0913 \approx 9.13\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.95$):

$$\binom{20}{18}(0.95)^{18}(0.05)^{2} \approx 0.1887$$

$$\binom{20}{19}(0.95)^{19}(0.05)^{1} \approx 0.3774$$

$$\binom{20}{20}(0.95)^{20}(0.05)^{0} \approx 0.3585$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 18) \approx 0.1887 + 0.3774 + 0.3585 = 0.9245 \approx 92.45\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 18)}{P_A(X \ge 18)} \approx \frac{92.45\%}{9.13\%} \approx 10.13$$

Since $10.13 > 10$, the statement is True.

**D.** Inspector A's variance in number of correctly classified items is more than 4 times Inspector B's variance. → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.75$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 20 \cdot 0.75 \cdot 0.25 = 3.75$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.95$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 20 \cdot 0.95 \cdot 0.05 = 0.95$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{3.75}{0.95} \approx 3.95$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is False.

**E.** On average, Inspector A does not meet the certification bar of 18 correctly classified items. → True

In this problem we have a binomial setting with $n = 20$ independent trials. Side A has success probability $p_A = 0.75$, and side B has $p_B = 0.95$. A success threshold of at least $k = 18$ successes is used in the scenario. Original wording: A factory runs a quality check on 20 items per batch. Inspector A is newly trained (p = 0.75 of correctly classifying each item). Inspector B is experienced (p = 0.95). Certification for a batch requires correctly classifying at least 18 of the 20 items.

Putting that against the claim, the statement is True.

tasks.title: First-Contact Resolutions
tasks.context: A call center tracks whether calls are resolved on the first contact, out of 15 calls per shift. Agent A is a trainee (p = 0.60 per call). Agent B is a senior agent (p = 0.88 per call). A performance bonus requires resolving at least 13 of the 15 calls on first contact. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Agent B's probability of resolving all 15 calls on first contact is greater than 15%.
The probability that Agent A qualifies for the bonus (at least 13 of 15 resolved) equals the sum, from x = 13 to 15, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 15 and p = 0.60.
Agent B is more than 25 times as likely as Agent A to qualify for the bonus.
Agent A's number of first-contact resolutions has a standard deviation greater than 2.
The expected number of calls resolved by Agent B (13.2) exceeds the bonus threshold of 13.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Agent B's probability of resolving all 15 calls on first contact is greater than 15%. → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.88$ and $n = 15$:

$$P(X = 15) = (0.88)^{15} \approx 0.146974 \approx 14.7\%$$

The claim compares this with $15\%$. We got about $14.6974\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** The probability that Agent A qualifies for the bonus (at least 13 of 15 resolved) equals the sum, from x = 13 to 15, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 15 and p = 0.60. → True

“At least 13 out of 15” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 13, 14, \ldots, 15$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 13) = P(X=13) + P(X=14) + \cdots + P(X=15) = \sum_{x=13}^{15} \binom{15}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{15-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 13)$ would only capture “exactly 13” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 15$ and $p = 0.6$, running from $x = 13$ to $x = 15$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Agent B is more than 25 times as likely as Agent A to qualify for the bonus. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 13 successes out of 15. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 13, 14, \ldots, 15$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 13) = \sum_{x=13}^{15} \binom{15}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{15-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 13)$ would only count “exactly 13” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.6$):

$$\binom{15}{13}(0.6)^{13}(0.4)^{2} \approx 0.0219$$

$$\binom{15}{14}(0.6)^{14}(0.4)^{1} \approx 0.0047$$

$$\binom{15}{15}(0.6)^{15}(0.4)^{0} \approx 0.0005$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 13) \approx 0.0219 + 0.0047 + 0.0005 = 0.0271 \approx 2.71\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.88$):

$$\binom{15}{13}(0.88)^{13}(0.12)^{2} \approx 0.287$$

$$\binom{15}{14}(0.88)^{14}(0.12)^{1} \approx 0.3006$$

$$\binom{15}{15}(0.88)^{15}(0.12)^{0} \approx 0.147$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 13) \approx 0.287 + 0.3006 + 0.147 = 0.7346 \approx 73.46\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 13)}{P_A(X \ge 13)} \approx \frac{73.46\%}{2.71\%} \approx 27.09$$

Since $27.09 > 25$, the statement is True.

**D.** Agent A's number of first-contact resolutions has a standard deviation greater than 2. → False

The standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance. For $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$,

$$\mathrm{SD}(X) = \sqrt{np(1-p)}$$

Side A ($p_A = 0.6$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 3.6, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(A) = \sqrt{3.6} \approx 1.897$$

Side B ($p_B = 0.88$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 1.584, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(B) = \sqrt{1.584} \approx 1.259$$

Comparing $1.897$ with $1.259$, the statement is False.

**E.** The expected number of calls resolved by Agent B (13.2) exceeds the bonus threshold of 13. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 15 \cdot 0.6 = 9$$

$$E[B] = 15 \cdot 0.88 = 13.2$$

The difference $E[B] - E[A] = 4.2$, and equivalently $n(p_B - p_A) = 15\cdot(0.88 - 0.6) = 4.2$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

tasks.title: Seed Germination Trays
tasks.context: A gardener plants trays of 12 seeds. Seed Batch A is old stock (p = 0.40 germination chance per seed). Seed Batch B is fresh stock (p = 0.85). A tray counts as a "full-tray success" if at least 10 of the 12 seeds germinate. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Seed Batch A has less than a 1-in-1000 (0.1%) chance of all 12 seeds germinating.
The probability that Batch B achieves a full-tray success (at least 10 of 12 germinate) equals the sum, from x = 10 to 12, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 12 and p = 0.85.
Batch B is more than 300 times as likely as Batch A to achieve a full-tray success.
Batch A has a lower variance in number of germinated seeds than Batch B.
The mean number of germinated seeds for Batch B is more than double the mean for Batch A.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Seed Batch A has less than a 1-in-1000 (0.1%) chance of all 12 seeds germinating. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.4$ and $n = 12$:

$$P(X = 12) = (0.4)^{12} \approx 1.6777 \times 10^{-5} \approx 0\%$$

Comparing this value with the claim shows the statement is True.

**B.** The probability that Batch B achieves a full-tray success (at least 10 of 12 germinate) equals the sum, from x = 10 to 12, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 12 and p = 0.85. → True

“At least 10 out of 12” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 10, 11, \ldots, 12$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 10) = P(X=10) + P(X=11) + \cdots + P(X=12) = \sum_{x=10}^{12} \binom{12}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{12-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 10)$ would only capture “exactly 10” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 12$ and $p = 0.85$, running from $x = 10$ to $x = 12$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Batch B is more than 300 times as likely as Batch A to achieve a full-tray success. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 10 successes out of 12. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 10, 11, \ldots, 12$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 10) = \sum_{x=10}^{12} \binom{12}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{12-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 10)$ would only count “exactly 10” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.4$):

$$\binom{12}{10}(0.4)^{10}(0.6)^{2} \approx 0.0025$$

$$\binom{12}{11}(0.4)^{11}(0.6)^{1} \approx 0.0003$$

$$\binom{12}{12}(0.4)^{12}(0.6)^{0} \approx 1.6777 \times 10^{-5}$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.0025 + 0.0003 + 1.6777 \times 10^{-5} = 0.0028 \approx 0.28\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.85$):

$$\binom{12}{10}(0.85)^{10}(0.15)^{2} \approx 0.2924$$

$$\binom{12}{11}(0.85)^{11}(0.15)^{1} \approx 0.3012$$

$$\binom{12}{12}(0.85)^{12}(0.15)^{0} \approx 0.1422$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 10) \approx 0.2924 + 0.3012 + 0.1422 = 0.7358 \approx 73.58\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 10)}{P_A(X \ge 10)} \approx \frac{73.58\%}{0.28\%} \approx 261.84$$

Since $261.84 \le 300$, the statement is False.

**D.** Batch A has a lower variance in number of germinated seeds than Batch B. → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.4$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 12 \cdot 0.4 \cdot 0.6 = 2.88$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.85$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 12 \cdot 0.85 \cdot 0.15 = 1.53$$

So $\mathrm{Var}(A) = 2.88$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 1.53$. The claim’s comparison is incorrect, so the statement is False.

**E.** The mean number of germinated seeds for Batch B is more than double the mean for Batch A. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 12 \cdot 0.4 = 4.8$$

$$E[B] = 12 \cdot 0.85 = 10.2$$

The ratio $E[B]/E[A] = 2.125$ (double would be $2$).

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

tasks.title: Airport Security Audit
tasks.context: An airport screens 25 test bags per audit. Agent A is newly certified (p = 0.70 of correctly flagging a prohibited item). Agent B is a veteran (p = 0.93). To pass the audit, an agent must correctly flag at least 23 of the 25 bags. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Agent A's probability of a flawless screening run (correctly flagging all 25 bags) is less than 0.01%.
The probability that Agent B passes the audit (at least 23 of 25 correctly flagged) equals the sum, from x = 23 to 25, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 25 and p = 0.93.
Agent B is more than 80 times as likely as Agent A to pass the audit.
Agent A's variance in number of correctly flagged bags is more than triple Agent B's variance.
The mean number of correctly flagged bags for Agent B is more than 35% higher than for Agent A.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Agent A's probability of a flawless screening run (correctly flagging all 25 bags) is less than 0.01%. → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.7$ and $n = 25$:

$$P(X = 25) = (0.7)^{25} \approx 0.000134 \approx 0.01\%$$

The claim compares this with $0.01\%$. We got about $0.0134\%$, which is above the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** The probability that Agent B passes the audit (at least 23 of 25 correctly flagged) equals the sum, from x = 23 to 25, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 25 and p = 0.93. → True

“At least 23 out of 25” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 23, 24, \ldots, 25$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 23) = P(X=23) + P(X=24) + \cdots + P(X=25) = \sum_{x=23}^{25} \binom{25}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{25-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 23)$ would only capture “exactly 23” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 25$ and $p = 0.93$, running from $x = 23$ to $x = 25$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Agent B is more than 80 times as likely as Agent A to pass the audit. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 23 successes out of 25. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 23, 24, \ldots, 25$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 23) = \sum_{x=23}^{25} \binom{25}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{25-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 23)$ would only count “exactly 23” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.7$):

$$\binom{25}{23}(0.7)^{23}(0.3)^{2} \approx 0.0074$$

$$\binom{25}{24}(0.7)^{24}(0.3)^{1} \approx 0.0014$$

$$\binom{25}{25}(0.7)^{25}(0.3)^{0} \approx 0.0001$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 23) \approx 0.0074 + 0.0014 + 0.0001 = 0.009 \approx 0.9\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.93$):

$$\binom{25}{23}(0.93)^{23}(0.07)^{2} \approx 0.277$$

$$\binom{25}{24}(0.93)^{24}(0.07)^{1} \approx 0.3066$$

$$\binom{25}{25}(0.93)^{25}(0.07)^{0} \approx 0.163$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 23) \approx 0.277 + 0.3066 + 0.163 = 0.7466 \approx 74.66\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 23)}{P_A(X \ge 23)} \approx \frac{74.66\%}{0.9\%} \approx 83.32$$

Since $83.32 > 80$, the statement is True.

**D.** Agent A's variance in number of correctly flagged bags is more than triple Agent B's variance. → True

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.7$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 25 \cdot 0.7 \cdot 0.3 = 5.25$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.93$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 25 \cdot 0.93 \cdot 0.07 = 1.6275$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{5.25}{1.6275} \approx 3.23$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** The mean number of correctly flagged bags for Agent B is more than 35% higher than for Agent A. → False

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 25 \cdot 0.7 = 17.5$$

$$E[B] = 25 \cdot 0.93 = 23.25$$

The percent increase of B over A is $100\big(E[B]/E[A] - 1\big) = 100\big(1.3286 - 1\big) \approx 32.86\%$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is False.

An airport screens 25 test bags per audit. Agent A is newly certified (p = 0.70 of correctly flagging a prohibited item). Agent B is a veteran (p = 0.93). To pass the audit, an agent must correctly flag at least 23 of the 25 bags.

We model each side as a binomial count with $n = 25$ independent trials: side A has success probability $p_A = 0.7$, side B has $p_B = 0.93$.

The scenario’s success cutoff is at least $k = 23$ successes out of $n = 25$.

tasks.title: Archery Medal Round
tasks.context: An archery competition awards a medal for hitting at least 8 bullseyes out of 9 arrows. Archer A is intermediate (p = 0.65 per arrow). Archer B is elite (p = 0.97 per arrow). Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Archer B's probability of a perfect round (9 for 9 bullseyes) is greater than 75%.

The expected number of bullseyes for Archer B is at least 3 more than for Archer A.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Archer B's probability of a perfect round (9 for 9 bullseyes) is greater than 75%. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.97$ and $n = 9$:

$$P(X = 9) = (0.97)^{9} \approx 0.760231 \approx 76.02\%$$

The claim compares this with $75\%$. We got about $76.0231\%$, which is above the cutoff, so the statement is True.

**B.** The probability that Archer A earns the medal (at least 8 of 9 bullseyes) equals the sum, from x = 8 to 9, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 9 and p = 0.65. → True

“At least 8 out of 9” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 8, 9, \ldots, 9$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 8) = P(X=8) + P(X=9) = \sum_{x=8}^{9} \binom{9}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{9-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 8)$ would only capture “exactly 8” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 9$ and $p = 0.65$, running from $x = 8$ to $x = 9$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Archer B is more than 8 times as likely as Archer A to earn the medal. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 8 successes out of 9. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 8, 9, \ldots, 9$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 8) = \sum_{x=8}^{9} \binom{9}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{9-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 8)$ would only count “exactly 8” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.65$):

$$\binom{9}{8}(0.65)^{8}(0.35)^{1} \approx 0.1004$$

$$\binom{9}{9}(0.65)^{9}(0.35)^{0} \approx 0.0207$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 8) \approx 0.1004 + 0.0207 = 0.1211 \approx 12.11\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.97$):

$$\binom{9}{8}(0.97)^{8}(0.03)^{1} \approx 0.2116$$

$$\binom{9}{9}(0.97)^{9}(0.03)^{0} \approx 0.7602$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 8) \approx 0.2116 + 0.7602 = 0.9718 \approx 97.18\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 8)}{P_A(X \ge 8)} \approx \frac{97.18\%}{12.11\%} \approx 8.03$$

Since $8.03 > 8$, the statement is True.

**D.** Archer A's variance in number of bullseyes is more than 8 times Archer B's variance. → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.65$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 9 \cdot 0.65 \cdot 0.35 = 2.0475$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.97$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 9 \cdot 0.97 \cdot 0.03 = 0.2619$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{2.0475}{0.2619} \approx 7.82$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is False.

**E.** The expected number of bullseyes for Archer B is at least 3 more than for Archer A. → False

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 9 \cdot 0.65 = 5.85$$

$$E[B] = 9 \cdot 0.97 = 8.73$$

The difference $E[B] - E[A] = 2.88$, and equivalently $n(p_B - p_A) = 9\cdot(0.97 - 0.65) = 2.88$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is False.

tasks.context: Two restaurants survey 14 customers each about satisfaction. Restaurant A is new (p = 0.50 of a customer being satisfied). Restaurant B is established (p = 0.80). A "good rating" requires at least 11 of the 14 customers satisfied. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Restaurant B's probability of a perfect run (all 14 customers satisfied) is greater than 5%.
The probability that Restaurant A earns a good rating (at least 11 of 14 satisfied) equals the sum, from x = 11 to 14, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 14 and p = 0.50.
Restaurant B is more than 20 times as likely as Restaurant A to earn a good rating.
Restaurant A has a lower variance in number of satisfied customers than Restaurant B.
The expected number of satisfied customers for Restaurant B is exactly 60% higher than for Restaurant A.

**A.** Restaurant B's probability of a perfect run (all 14 customers satisfied) is greater than 5%. → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.8$ and $n = 14$:

$$P(X = 14) = (0.8)^{14} \approx 0.04398 \approx 4.4\%$$

The claim compares this with $5\%$. We got about $4.398\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** The probability that Restaurant A earns a good rating (at least 11 of 14 satisfied) equals the sum, from x = 11 to 14, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 14 and p = 0.50. → True

“At least 11 out of 14” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 11, 12, \ldots, 14$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 11) = P(X=11) + P(X=12) + \cdots + P(X=14) = \sum_{x=11}^{14} \binom{14}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{14-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 11)$ would only capture “exactly 11” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 14$ and $p = 0.5$, running from $x = 11$ to $x = 14$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Restaurant B is more than 20 times as likely as Restaurant A to earn a good rating. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 11 successes out of 14. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 11, 12, \ldots, 14$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 11) = \sum_{x=11}^{14} \binom{14}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{14-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 11)$ would only count “exactly 11” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.5$):

$$\binom{14}{11}(0.5)^{11}(0.5)^{3} \approx 0.0222$$

$$\binom{14}{12}(0.5)^{12}(0.5)^{2} \approx 0.0056$$

$$\binom{14}{13}(0.5)^{13}(0.5)^{1} \approx 0.0009$$

$$\binom{14}{14}(0.5)^{14}(0.5)^{0} \approx 6.1035 \times 10^{-5}$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 11) \approx 0.0222 + 0.0056 + 0.0009 + 6.1035 \times 10^{-5} = 0.0287 \approx 2.87\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.8$):

$$\binom{14}{11}(0.8)^{11}(0.2)^{3} \approx 0.2501$$

$$\binom{14}{12}(0.8)^{12}(0.2)^{2} \approx 0.2501$$

$$\binom{14}{13}(0.8)^{13}(0.2)^{1} \approx 0.1539$$

$$\binom{14}{14}(0.8)^{14}(0.2)^{0} \approx 0.044$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 11) \approx 0.2501 + 0.2501 + 0.1539 + 0.044 = 0.6982 \approx 69.82\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 11)}{P_A(X \ge 11)} \approx \frac{69.82\%}{2.87\%} \approx 24.34$$

Since $24.34 > 20$, the statement is True.

**D.** Restaurant A has a lower variance in number of satisfied customers than Restaurant B. → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.5$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 14 \cdot 0.5 \cdot 0.5 = 3.5$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.8$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 14 \cdot 0.8 \cdot 0.2 = 2.24$$

So $\mathrm{Var}(A) = 3.5$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 2.24$. The claim’s comparison is incorrect, so the statement is False.

**E.** The expected number of satisfied customers for Restaurant B is exactly 60% higher than for Restaurant A. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 14 \cdot 0.5 = 7$$

$$E[B] = 14 \cdot 0.8 = 11.2$$

The percent increase of B over A is $100\big(E[B]/E[A] - 1\big) = 100\big(1.6 - 1\big) \approx 60\%$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

tasks.title: Phishing Awareness Test
tasks.context: A company runs a phishing-email test with 18 emails. Staff A is untrained (p = 0.45 of correctly identifying a phishing email). Staff B is trained (p = 0.91). Passing the security review requires correctly identifying at least 16 of the 18 emails. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Staff A's probability of perfectly identifying all 18 phishing emails is less than 0.001%.
The probability that Staff B passes the security review (at least 16 of 18 correctly identified) equals the sum, from x = 16 to 18, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 18 and p = 0.91.
Staff B is more than 6,000 times as likely as Staff A to pass the security review.

**A.** Staff A's probability of perfectly identifying all 18 phishing emails is less than 0.001%. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.45$ and $n = 18$:

$$P(X = 18) = (0.45)^{18} \approx 5.7257 \times 10^{-7} \approx 5.7257 \times 10^{-5}\%$$

$$P(X \ge 16) = P(X=16) + P(X=17) + \cdots + P(X=18) = \sum_{x=16}^{18} \binom{18}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{18-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 16)$ would only capture “exactly 16” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 18$ and $p = 0.91$, running from $x = 16$ to $x = 18$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Staff B is more than 6,000 times as likely as Staff A to pass the security review. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 16 successes out of 18. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 16, 17, \ldots, 18$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 16) = \sum_{x=16}^{18} \binom{18}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{18-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 16)$ would only count “exactly 16” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.45$):

$$\binom{18}{17}(0.91)^{17}(0.09)^{1} \approx 0.326$$

$$\binom{18}{18}(0.91)^{18}(0.09)^{0} \approx 0.1831$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 16) \approx 0.2741 + 0.326 + 0.1831 = 0.7832 \approx 78.32\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 16)}{P_A(X \ge 16)} \approx \frac{78.32\%}{0.01\%} \approx 5437.54$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.91$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 18 \cdot 0.91 \cdot 0.09 = 1.4742$$

The variance ratio is

**B.** The probability that Meteorologist A wins the accuracy award (at least 9 of 10 correct) equals the sum, from x = 9 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.60. → True

“At least 9 out of 10” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 9, 10, \ldots, 10$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 9) = P(X=9) + P(X=10) = \sum_{x=9}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 9)$ would only capture “exactly 9” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.6$, running from $x = 9$ to $x = 10$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Meteorologist B is more than 20 times as likely as Meteorologist A to win the accuracy award. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 9 successes out of 10. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 9, 10, \ldots, 10$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 9) = \sum_{x=9}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 9)$ would only count “exactly 9” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.6$):

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.6)^{9}(0.4)^{1} \approx 0.0403$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.6)^{10}(0.4)^{0} \approx 0.006$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 9) \approx 0.0403 + 0.006 = 0.0464 \approx 4.64\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.95$):

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.95)^{9}(0.05)^{1} \approx 0.3151$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.95)^{10}(0.05)^{0} \approx 0.5987$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 9) \approx 0.3151 + 0.5987 = 0.9139 \approx 91.39\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 9)}{P_A(X \ge 9)} \approx \frac{91.39\%}{4.64\%} \approx 19.71$$

Since $19.71 \le 20$, the statement is False.

**D.** Meteorologist A's variance in number of correct forecasts is more than 5 times Meteorologist B's variance. → True

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.6$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 10 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.4 = 2.4$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.95$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 10 \cdot 0.95 \cdot 0.05 = 0.475$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{2.4}{0.475} \approx 5.05$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** The expected number of correct forecasts for Meteorologist B exceeds Meteorologist A's by more than 3. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 10 \cdot 0.6 = 6$$

$$E[B] = 10 \cdot 0.95 = 9.5$$

The difference $E[B] - E[A] = 3.5$, and equivalently $n(p_B - p_A) = 10\cdot(0.95 - 0.6) = 3.5$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

Clearing the cutoff means at least 17 successes out of 20. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 17, 18, \ldots, 20$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$\binom{20}{20}(0.88)^{20}(0.12)^{0} \approx 0.0776$$

The variance ratio is

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is True.

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

The percent increase of B over A is $100\big(E[B]/E[A] - 1\big) = 100\big(1.6 - 1\big) \approx 60\%$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is False.

tasks.title: Typing Accuracy Test
tasks.context: Two applicants take a 12-question typing accuracy test. Typist A is a beginner (p = 0.50 of typing a line correctly). Typist B is experienced (p = 0.75). Passing the test requires typing at least 9 of the 12 lines correctly. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Typist B's probability of a flawless test (all 12 lines correct) is greater than 3%.

The expected number of lines correct for Typist B is exactly 50% higher than for Typist A.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Typist B's probability of a flawless test (all 12 lines correct) is greater than 3%. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.75$ and $n = 12$:

$$P(X = 12) = (0.75)^{12} \approx 0.031676 \approx 3.17\%$$

The claim compares this with $3\%$. We got about $3.1676\%$, which is above the cutoff, so the statement is True.

**B.** The probability that Typist A passes the test (at least 9 of 12 correct) equals the sum, from x = 9 to 12, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 12 and p = 0.50. → True

“At least 9 out of 12” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 9, 10, \ldots, 12$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 9) = P(X=9) + P(X=10) + \cdots + P(X=12) = \sum_{x=9}^{12} \binom{12}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{12-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 9)$ would only capture “exactly 9” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 12$ and $p = 0.5$, running from $x = 9$ to $x = 12$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Typist B is more than 9 times as likely as Typist A to pass the test. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 9 successes out of 12. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 9, 10, \ldots, 12$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 9) = \sum_{x=9}^{12} \binom{12}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{12-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 9)$ would only count “exactly 9” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

$$\binom{12}{11}(0.5)^{11}(0.5)^{1} \approx 0.0029$$

$$\binom{12}{12}(0.5)^{12}(0.5)^{0} \approx 0.0002$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$\binom{12}{10}(0.75)^{10}(0.25)^{2} \approx 0.2323$$

$$\binom{12}{11}(0.75)^{11}(0.25)^{1} \approx 0.1267$$

$$\binom{12}{12}(0.75)^{12}(0.25)^{0} \approx 0.0317$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.4$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 22 \cdot 0.4 \cdot 0.6 = 5.28$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.89$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 22 \cdot 0.89 \cdot 0.11 = 2.1538$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{5.28}{2.1538} \approx 2.45$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is False.

**E.** The mean number of correctly identified attacks for Staff B is more than double the mean for Staff A. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 22 \cdot 0.4 = 8.8$$

$$E[B] = 22 \cdot 0.89 = 19.58$$

The ratio $E[B]/E[A] = 2.225$ (double would be $2$).

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

tasks.title: Eight Free Throws Contest
tasks.context: Two basketball players each attempt 8 free throws in a shooting contest. Player A is a solid shooter (p = 0.55 per attempt). Player B is an elite shooter (p = 0.90 per attempt). An award requires making at least 7 of the 8 free throws. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Player B's probability of a perfect round (8 for 8 free throws) is greater than 45%.
The probability that Player B earns the award (at least 7 of 8 made) equals the sum, from x = 7 to 8, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 8 and p = 0.90.
Player B is more than 12 times as likely as Player A to earn the award.
Player A's variance in number of free throws made is more than triple Player B's variance.
The expected number of free throws made by Player B exceeds Player A's by more than 3.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Player B's probability of a perfect round (8 for 8 free throws) is greater than 45%. → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.9$ and $n = 8$:

$$P(X = 8) = (0.9)^{8} \approx 0.430467 \approx 43.05\%$$

The claim compares this with $45\%$. We got about $43.0467\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** The probability that Player B earns the award (at least 7 of 8 made) equals the sum, from x = 7 to 8, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 8 and p = 0.90. → True

“At least 7 out of 8” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 7, 8, \ldots, 8$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 7) = P(X=7) + P(X=8) = \sum_{x=7}^{8} \binom{8}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{8-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 7)$ would only capture “exactly 7” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 8$ and $p = 0.9$, running from $x = 7$ to $x = 8$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Player B is more than 12 times as likely as Player A to earn the award. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 7 successes out of 8. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 7, 8, \ldots, 8$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 7) = \sum_{x=7}^{8} \binom{8}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{8-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 7)$ would only count “exactly 7” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.55$):

$$\binom{8}{7}(0.55)^{7}(0.45)^{1} \approx 0.0548$$

$$\binom{8}{8}(0.55)^{8}(0.45)^{0} \approx 0.0084$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 7) \approx 0.0548 + 0.0084 = 0.0632 \approx 6.32\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.9$):

$$\binom{8}{7}(0.9)^{7}(0.1)^{1} \approx 0.3826$$

$$\binom{8}{8}(0.9)^{8}(0.1)^{0} \approx 0.4305$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 7) \approx 0.3826 + 0.4305 = 0.8131 \approx 81.31\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 7)}{P_A(X \ge 7)} \approx \frac{81.31\%}{6.32\%} \approx 12.87$$

Since $12.87 > 12$, the statement is True.

**D.** Player A's variance in number of free throws made is more than triple Player B's variance. → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.55$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 8 \cdot 0.55 \cdot 0.45 = 1.98$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.9$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 8 \cdot 0.9 \cdot 0.1 = 0.72$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{1.98}{0.72} \approx 2.75$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is False.

**E.** The expected number of free throws made by Player B exceeds Player A's by more than 3. → False

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 8 \cdot 0.55 = 4.4$$

$$E[B] = 8 \cdot 0.9 = 7.2$$

The difference $E[B] - E[A] = 2.8$, and equivalently $n(p_B - p_A) = 8\cdot(0.9 - 0.55) = 2.8$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is False.

tasks.title: Diagnostic Kit Certification
tasks.context: A lab tests two diagnostic kits on 15 known-positive samples. Kit A is an older model (p = 0.65 of correctly detecting a positive sample). Kit B is a newer model (p = 0.94). A kit is certified if it correctly detects at least 13 of the 15 samples. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.

Kit A's standard deviation in number of correct detections is more than twice Kit B's standard deviation.
The mode (most likely single number of correct detections) for Kit A is 9.

$$P(X = 0) = (1-p)^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.65$, so $1-p = 0.35$ and $n = 15$:

$$P(X = 0) = (0.35)^{15} \approx 1.4488 \times 10^{-7} \approx 1.4488 \times 10^{-5}\%$$

**B.** The probability that Kit B is certified (at least 13 of 15 correctly detected) equals the sum, from x = 13 to 15, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 15 and p = 0.94. → True

“At least 13 out of 15” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 13, 14, \ldots, 15$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 13) = P(X=13) + P(X=14) + \cdots + P(X=15) = \sum_{x=13}^{15} \binom{15}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{15-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 13)$ would only capture “exactly 13” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 15$ and $p = 0.94$, running from $x = 13$ to $x = 15$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Kit B is more than 15 times as likely as Kit A to be certified. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 13 successes out of 15. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 13, 14, \ldots, 15$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 13) = \sum_{x=13}^{15} \binom{15}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{15-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 13)$ would only count “exactly 13” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.65$):

$$\binom{15}{13}(0.65)^{13}(0.35)^{2} \approx 0.0476$$

$$\binom{15}{14}(0.65)^{14}(0.35)^{1} \approx 0.0126$$

$$\binom{15}{15}(0.65)^{15}(0.35)^{0} \approx 0.0016$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 13) \approx 0.0476 + 0.0126 + 0.0016 = 0.0617 \approx 6.17\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.94$):

$$\binom{15}{13}(0.94)^{13}(0.06)^{2} \approx 0.1691$$

$$\binom{15}{14}(0.94)^{14}(0.06)^{1} \approx 0.3785$$

$$\binom{15}{15}(0.94)^{15}(0.06)^{0} \approx 0.3953$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 13) \approx 0.1691 + 0.3785 + 0.3953 = 0.9429 \approx 94.29\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 13)}{P_A(X \ge 13)} \approx \frac{94.29\%}{6.17\%} \approx 15.27$$

Since $15.27 > 15$, the statement is True.

**D.** Kit A's standard deviation in number of correct detections is more than twice Kit B's standard deviation. → True

The standard deviation is the positive square root of the variance. For $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$,

$$\mathrm{SD}(X) = \sqrt{np(1-p)}$$

Side A ($p_A = 0.65$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 3.4125, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(A) = \sqrt{3.4125} \approx 1.847$$

Side B ($p_B = 0.94$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 0.846, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(B) = \sqrt{0.846} \approx 0.92$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{SD}(A)}{\mathrm{SD}(B)} \approx \frac{1.847}{0.92} \approx 2.008$$

Against the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** The mode (most likely single number of correct detections) for Kit A is 9. → False

The mode is the integer $k$ that maximizes $P(X = k)$. For $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ it is $\lfloor (n+1)p \rfloor$ (or two adjacent integers when $(n+1)p$ is an integer).

In this problem we have a binomial setting with $n = 15$ independent trials. Side A has success probability $p_A = 0.65$, and side B has $p_B = 0.94$. A success threshold of at least $k = 13$ successes is used in the scenario. Original wording: A lab tests two diagnostic kits on 15 known-positive samples. Kit A is an older model (p = 0.65 of correctly detecting a positive sample). Kit B is a newer model (p = 0.94). A kit is certified if it correctly detects at least 13 of the 15 samples.

Putting that against the claim, the statement is False.

The probability of exactly 12 successful procedures, P(X = 12), is higher for Surgeon A than for Surgeon B.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Surgeon B's probability of a flawless year (all 14 procedures successful) is more than 30 times Surgeon A's flawless-year probability. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.96$ and $n = 14$:

$$P(X = 14) = (0.96)^{14} \approx 0.564673 \approx 56.47\%$$

Comparing this value with the claim shows the statement is True.

**B.** The probability that Surgeon A meets the benchmark (at least 12 of 14 successful) equals the sum, from x = 12 to 14, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 14 and p = 0.75. → True

“At least 12 out of 14” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 12, 13, \ldots, 14$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 12) = P(X=12) + P(X=13) + \cdots + P(X=14) = \sum_{x=12}^{14} \binom{14}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{14-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 12)$ would only capture “exactly 12” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 14$ and $p = 0.75$, running from $x = 12$ to $x = 14$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Surgeon B is more than 3.5 times as likely as Surgeon A to meet the benchmark. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 12 successes out of 14. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 12, 13, \ldots, 14$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 12) = \sum_{x=12}^{14} \binom{14}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{14-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 12)$ would only count “exactly 12” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

$$\binom{14}{12}(0.75)^{12}(0.25)^{2} \approx 0.1802$$

$$\binom{14}{13}(0.75)^{13}(0.25)^{1} \approx 0.0832$$

$$\binom{14}{14}(0.75)^{14}(0.25)^{0} \approx 0.0178$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 12) \approx 0.1802 + 0.0832 + 0.0178 = 0.2811 \approx 28.11\%$$

$$\binom{14}{12}(0.96)^{12}(0.04)^{2} \approx 0.0892$$

$$\binom{14}{13}(0.96)^{13}(0.04)^{1} \approx 0.3294$$

$$\binom{14}{14}(0.96)^{14}(0.04)^{0} \approx 0.5647$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 12) \approx 0.0892 + 0.3294 + 0.5647 = 0.9833 \approx 98.33\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 12)}{P_A(X \ge 12)} \approx \frac{98.33\%}{28.11\%} \approx 3.5$$

Matching this ratio to the claim, the statement is False.

**D.** Surgeon A's standard deviation in number of successes is more than double Surgeon B's standard deviation. → True

$$\mathrm{SD}(X) = \sqrt{np(1-p)}$$

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 2.625, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(A) = \sqrt{2.625} \approx 1.62$$

Side B ($p_B = 0.96$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 0.5376, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(B) = \sqrt{0.5376} \approx 0.733$$

$$\frac{\mathrm{SD}(A)}{\mathrm{SD}(B)} \approx \frac{1.62}{0.733} \approx 2.21$$

Against the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** The probability of exactly 12 successful procedures, P(X = 12), is higher for Surgeon A than for Surgeon B. → True

Putting that against the claim, the statement is False.

“At least 19 out of 22” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 19, 20, \ldots, 22$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 19) = P(X=19) + P(X=20) + \cdots + P(X=22) = \sum_{x=19}^{22} \binom{22}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{22-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 19)$ would only capture “exactly 19” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 22$ and $p = 0.65$, running from $x = 19$ to $x = 22$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Factory B is more than 30 times as likely as Factory A to have its batch pass. → True

Clearing the cutoff means at least 85 successes out of 22. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 85, 86, \ldots, 22$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 85) = \sum_{x=85}^{22} \binom{22}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{22-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 85)$ would only count “exactly 85” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 85) \approx  = 0 \approx 0\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.92$):

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 85) \approx  = 0 \approx 0\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 85)}{P_A(X \ge 85)} \approx \frac{0\%}{0\%} \approx \infty$$

Since $\infty > 30$, the statement is True.

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.22$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 35 \cdot 0.22 \cdot 0.78 = 6.006$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.78$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 35 \cdot 0.78 \cdot 0.22 = 6.006$$

So $\mathrm{Var}(A) = 6.006$ and $\mathrm{Var}(B) = 6.006$. The claim’s comparison is correct, so the statement is True.

Side B ($p_B = 0.78$):

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 6.006, \qquad \mathrm{SD}(B) = \sqrt{6.006} \approx 2.451$$

Comparing $2.451$ with $2.451$, the statement is False.

**C.** The probability that Check A flags exactly 0 components is equal to the probability that Check B flags all 35 components. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.78$ and $n = 35$:

$$P(X = 35) = (0.78)^{35} \approx 0.000167 \approx 0.02\%$$

Comparing this value with the claim shows the statement is True.

tasks.title: Bakery Quality Control
tasks.context: A bakery runs a quality-control check on 18 pastries per batch. Baker A is a trainee (p = 0.45 of correctly shaping a pastry to spec). Baker B is an expert (p = 0.85). To pass the check, a baker must correctly shape at least 15 of the 18 pastries. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Baker A's probability of a flawless batch (all 18 pastries correct) is less than 0.0001%.
The probability that Baker B passes the check (at least 15 of 18 correct) equals the sum, from x = 15 to 18, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 18 and p = 0.85.
Baker B is more than 750 times as likely as Baker A to pass the check.
Baker A's variance in number of correctly shaped pastries is more than double Baker B's variance.
The mean number of correctly shaped pastries for Baker B is more than 90% higher than for Baker A.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Baker A's probability of a flawless batch (all 18 pastries correct) is less than 0.0001%. → True

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side A, $p = 0.45$ and $n = 18$:

$$P(X = 18) = (0.45)^{18} \approx 5.7257 \times 10^{-7} \approx 5.7257 \times 10^{-5}\%$$

The claim compares this with $0.0001\%$. We got about $5.7257 \times 10^{-5}\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is True.

**B.** The probability that Baker B passes the check (at least 15 of 18 correct) equals the sum, from x = 15 to 18, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 18 and p = 0.85. → True

“At least 15 out of 18” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 15, 16, \ldots, 18$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 15) = P(X=15) + P(X=16) + \cdots + P(X=18) = \sum_{x=15}^{18} \binom{18}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{18-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 15)$ would only capture “exactly 15” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 18$ and $p = 0.85$, running from $x = 15$ to $x = 18$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Baker B is more than 750 times as likely as Baker A to pass the check. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 15 successes out of 18. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 15, 16, \ldots, 18$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 15) = \sum_{x=15}^{18} \binom{18}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{18-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 15)$ would only count “exactly 15” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.45$):

$$\binom{18}{15}(0.45)^{15}(0.55)^{3} \approx 0.0009$$

$$\binom{18}{16}(0.45)^{16}(0.55)^{2} \approx 0.0001$$

$$\binom{18}{17}(0.45)^{17}(0.55)^{1} \approx 1.2596 \times 10^{-5}$$

$$\binom{18}{18}(0.45)^{18}(0.55)^{0} \approx 5.7257 \times 10^{-7}$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 15) \approx 0.0009 + 0.0001 + 1.2596 \times 10^{-5} + 5.7257 \times 10^{-7} = 0.001 \approx 0.1\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.85$):

$$\binom{18}{15}(0.85)^{15}(0.15)^{3} \approx 0.2406$$

$$\binom{18}{16}(0.85)^{16}(0.15)^{2} \approx 0.2556$$

$$\binom{18}{17}(0.85)^{17}(0.15)^{1} \approx 0.1704$$

$$\binom{18}{18}(0.85)^{18}(0.15)^{0} \approx 0.0536$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 15) \approx 0.2406 + 0.2556 + 0.1704 + 0.0536 = 0.7202 \approx 72.02\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 15)}{P_A(X \ge 15)} \approx \frac{72.02\%}{0.1\%} \approx 722.36$$

Since $722.36 \le 750$, the statement is False.

**D.** Baker A's variance in number of correctly shaped pastries is more than double Baker B's variance. → False

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.45$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 18 \cdot 0.45 \cdot 0.55 = 4.455$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.85$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 18 \cdot 0.85 \cdot 0.15 = 2.295$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{4.455}{2.295} \approx 1.94$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is False.

**E.** The mean number of correctly shaped pastries for Baker B is more than 90% higher than for Baker A. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 18 \cdot 0.45 = 8.1$$

$$E[B] = 18 \cdot 0.85 = 15.3$$

The percent increase of B over A is $100\big(E[B]/E[A] - 1\big) = 100\big(1.8889 - 1\big) \approx 88.89\%$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

We model each side as a binomial count with $n = 18$ independent trials: side A has success probability $p_A = 0.45$, side B has $p_B = 0.85$.

The scenario’s success cutoff is at least $k = 15$ successes out of $n = 18$.

**B.** The probability that Tester B clears the gate (at least 22 of 25 correctly flagged) equals the sum, from x = 22 to 25, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 25 and p = 0.93. → True

$$P(X \ge 22) = P(X=22) + P(X=23) + \cdots + P(X=25) = \sum_{x=22}^{25} \binom{25}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{25-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 22)$ would only capture “exactly 22” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 25$ and $p = 0.93$, running from $x = 22$ to $x = 25$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Tester B is more than 15,000,000 times as likely as Tester A to clear the gate. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 22 successes out of 25. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 22, 23, \ldots, 25$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 22) = \sum_{x=22}^{25} \binom{25}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{25-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 22)$ would only count “exactly 22” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.35$):

$$\binom{25}{22}(0.35)^{22}(0.65)^{3} \approx 5.888 \times 10^{-8}$$

$$\binom{25}{23}(0.35)^{23}(0.65)^{2} \approx 4.1354 \times 10^{-9}$$

$$\binom{25}{24}(0.35)^{24}(0.65)^{1} \approx 1.8556 \times 10^{-10}$$

$$\binom{25}{25}(0.35)^{25}(0.65)^{0} \approx 3.9967 \times 10^{-12}$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 22) \approx 5.888 \times 10^{-8} + 4.1354 \times 10^{-9} + 1.8556 \times 10^{-10} + 3.9967 \times 10^{-12} = 6.3205 \times 10^{-8} \approx 6.3205 \times 10^{-6}\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.93$):

$$\binom{25}{22}(0.93)^{22}(0.07)^{3} \approx 0.1598$$

$$\binom{25}{23}(0.93)^{23}(0.07)^{2} \approx 0.277$$

$$\binom{25}{24}(0.93)^{24}(0.07)^{1} \approx 0.3066$$

$$\binom{25}{25}(0.93)^{25}(0.07)^{0} \approx 0.163$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 22) \approx 0.1598 + 0.277 + 0.3066 + 0.163 = 0.9064 \approx 90.64\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 22)}{P_A(X \ge 22)} \approx \frac{90.64\%}{6.3205 \times 10^{-6}\%} \approx 14340560.29$$

Since $14340560.29 \le 15000000$, the statement is False.

**D.** Tester A's variance in number of correctly flagged test cases is more than triple Tester B's variance. → True

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.35$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 25 \cdot 0.35 \cdot 0.65 = 5.6875$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.93$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 25 \cdot 0.93 \cdot 0.07 = 1.6275$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{5.6875}{1.6275} \approx 3.49$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** The mean number of correctly flagged test cases for Tester B is more than 170% higher than for Tester A. → False

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 25 \cdot 0.35 = 8.75$$

$$E[B] = 25 \cdot 0.93 = 23.25$$

The percent increase of B over A is $100\big(E[B]/E[A] - 1\big) = 100\big(2.6571 - 1\big) \approx 165.71\%$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is False.

We model each side as a binomial count with $n = 25$ independent trials: side A has success probability $p_A = 0.35$, side B has $p_B = 0.93$.

The scenario’s success cutoff is at least $k = 22$ successes out of $n = 25$.

tasks.title: Ten-Arrow Archery Contest
tasks.context: Two archers each shoot 10 arrows in a contest. Archer A is a club-level shooter (p = 0.60 per arrow). Archer B is an elite shooter (p = 0.95 per arrow). An award requires hitting the target on at least 9 of the 10 arrows. Evaluate each statement. Mark it TRUE or FALSE.
statements: Archer B's probability of a perfect round (10 for 10) is greater than 60%.
The probability that Archer B earns the award (at least 9 of 10 hits) equals the sum, from x = 9 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.95.
Archer B is more than 20 times as likely as Archer A to earn the award.
Archer A's variance in number of arrows hit is more than 5 times Archer B's variance.
The expected number of arrows hit by Archer B exceeds Archer A's by more than 3.
tactical_explanations:
**A.** Archer B's probability of a perfect round (10 for 10) is greater than 60%. → False

A perfect run means every one of the $n$ trials succeeds. Independence lets us multiply the success probability across all trials, which is the binomial PMF at $k = n$:

$$P(X = n) = p^{n}$$

For side B, $p = 0.95$ and $n = 10$:

$$P(X = 10) = (0.95)^{10} \approx 0.598737 \approx 59.87\%$$

The claim compares this with $60\%$. We got about $59.8737\%$, which is below the cutoff, so the statement is False.

**B.** The probability that Archer B earns the award (at least 9 of 10 hits) equals the sum, from x = 9 to 10, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 10 and p = 0.95. → True

“At least 9 out of 10” is not a single outcome — it covers the distinct counts $X = 9, 10, \ldots, 10$. Those counts cannot happen at the same time, so by the addition rule for mutually exclusive events we add their individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 9) = P(X=9) + P(X=10) = \sum_{x=9}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term such as $P(X = 9)$ would only capture “exactly 9” and would undercount the true chance of clearing the cutoff. The statement writes this sum with $n = 10$ and $p = 0.95$, running from $x = 9$ to $x = 10$ — which matches the English claim, so the statement is True.

**C.** Archer B is more than 20 times as likely as Archer A to earn the award. → False

Clearing the cutoff means at least 9 successes out of 10. That event is the union of the mutually exclusive outcomes $X = 9, 10, \ldots, 10$, so we add the individual binomial probabilities:

$$P(X \ge 9) = \sum_{x=9}^{10} \binom{10}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{10-x}$$

A single term $P(X = 9)$ would only count “exactly 9” and would miss the higher counts, so it understates the chance of meeting the cutoff. We need the full upper tail for each side, then the ratio of those two probabilities — not the ratio of the two $p$ values.

Side A ($p = 0.6$):

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.6)^{9}(0.4)^{1} \approx 0.0403$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.6)^{10}(0.4)^{0} \approx 0.006$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 9) \approx 0.0403 + 0.006 = 0.0464 \approx 4.64\%$$

Side B ($p = 0.95$):

$$\binom{10}{9}(0.95)^{9}(0.05)^{1} \approx 0.3151$$

$$\binom{10}{10}(0.95)^{10}(0.05)^{0} \approx 0.5987$$

Adding the mutually exclusive pieces:

$$P(X \ge 9) \approx 0.3151 + 0.5987 = 0.9139 \approx 91.39\%$$

The ratio in the claim’s order (B relative to A):

$$\frac{P_B(X \ge 9)}{P_A(X \ge 9)} \approx \frac{91.39\%}{4.64\%} \approx 19.71$$

Since $19.71 \le 20$, the statement is False.

**D.** Archer A's variance in number of arrows hit is more than 5 times Archer B's variance. → True

For a binomial count $X \sim \mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, write $X$ as the sum of $n$ independent Bernoulli($p$) indicators. Each indicator has variance $p(1-p)$, and variances of independent summands add, so

$$\mathrm{Var}(X) = np(1-p)$$

This is largest when $p$ is closest to $1/2$, not when $p$ itself is largest.

Side A with $p_A = 0.6$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(A) = 10 \cdot 0.6 \cdot 0.4 = 2.4$$

Side B with $p_B = 0.95$:

$$\mathrm{Var}(B) = 10 \cdot 0.95 \cdot 0.05 = 0.475$$

The variance ratio is

$$\frac{\mathrm{Var}(A)}{\mathrm{Var}(B)} = \frac{2.4}{0.475} \approx 5.05$$

Comparing that with the claim, the statement is True.

**E.** The expected number of arrows hit by Archer B exceeds Archer A's by more than 3. → True

The mean of a binomial count is the number of trials times the success probability, because $X$ is the sum of $n$ Bernoulli($p$) indicators each with mean $p$:

$$E[X] = np$$

$$E[A] = 10 \cdot 0.6 = 6$$

$$E[B] = 10 \cdot 0.95 = 9.5$$

The difference $E[B] - E[A] = 3.5$, and equivalently $n(p_B - p_A) = 10\cdot(0.95 - 0.6) = 3.5$.

Matching these figures to the claim, the statement is True.

**C.** Agent B is more than 70 times as likely as Agent A to pass the review. → False

tasks.title: Diagnostic Scan Review

statements: Radiologist A's probability of correctly reading all 30 scans is less than 0.0002%.

**B.** The probability that Radiologist B passes the drill (at least 27 of 30 correctly read) equals the sum, from x = 27 to 30, of the binomial probabilities P(X = x), using n = 30 and p = 0.97. → True

**C.** Radiologist B is more than 500 times as likely as Radiologist A to pass the drill. → True

$$P(X \ge 27) = \sum_{x=27}^{30} \binom{30}{x} p^{x} (1-p)^{30-x}$$
